Not going to link to Reddit, but here's a really good synopsis of the rulings and the conclusion.

Here's my summary of it, I wouldn't read too much into the scare quotes, Berman uses them all over the place.

  • First 18 pages provide a lengthy but even-handed summary of the factual background, mostly focusing on the investigation and appeals process. I won't summarize, I'm sure most of you are familiar with it.

  • Pages 18-20 provide the legal standard for reviewing an arbitration award.

  • Page 20 is where the analysis begins.

  • First sentence is that he accepts the Arbitrator's facts as he found them, which he is basically required to under current case law.

  • The Court's decision rests primarily on the lack of notice given to Brady that he would be suspended for four games for being "generally aware" of a scheme to tamper with the balls or for noncooperation. Notice is required under the "law of the shop" (i.e. what the CBA, as interpreted, requires). Four games is the suspension for steroid use, and is not an adequate comparison. No previous player has been punished for "general awareness" of someone else's violation.

  • On Brady's non-cooperation, Judge Berman cited to Wells' testimony that he told Brady he would not be punished for not handing over his cell phone and emails. He also cites to the arbitration award in BountyGate, when Tagliabue said there was no "record of past suspensions based purely on obstructing a League investigation."

  • No notice that "generally aware" is punishable conduct. No player has previously been punished for something like that.

  • Only notice of fines for equipment violations, not a suspension. The Competitive Integrity Policy regulates ball pressures, and therefore regulates clubs, but does not regulate players, and Brady did not have notice of it.

  • What about conduct detrimental? Rice and Peterson "could, perhaps, be said to appreciate that acts of domestic violence might be deemed 'conduct detrimental.'" But even then, they were only disciplined under the new Personal Conduct policy. Similarly, there is a specific provision for equipment tampering that "is better calculated to provide notice to a player than a general concept such as 'conduct detrimental.'"

  • Denying Pash's testimony was "fundamentally unfair." But arbitrator must give each side "adequate opportunity to present its evidence and argument." NFL precedent must allow players to confront their investigators. Pash was co-lead of the investigation and would have had "valuable insight" in the Investigation and the drafting of the report. You can't use Wells' testimony to conclude Pash's edits to the report weren't "that big a deal," since Wells hadn't seen Pash's edits. You need Pash's testimony to determine the content of the edits, and whether the investigation was independent.

  • Goodell improperly denied Brady access to the notes from the Wells' investigation. Without the interview notes, Brady "was denied an opportunity to examine and challenge materials that may have led to his suspension." Of note was that Paul Weiss attorneys conducted the witness examinations at the appeals hearing, and with access to interview notes, "was able to use them in direct and cross-examinations of Brady and other arbitration witnesses."

  • The Court does not reach Brady's other claims.

Initial thoughts: big win for Pats fans. Not so sure it's a big win for Brady, since the Judge didn't disturb the factual findings and appears to suggest a monetary fine would have been appropriate. Though how the public will interpret the order remains to be seen (I believe most people will say it exonerated Brady). Not actually the worst thing in the world for the NFL. What they lose:

  • They lose a quite a bit of flexibility in punishing players under "conduct detrimental," especially if some other provision appears to better govern that conduct.

  • They can't punish for noncooperation.

  • They need to tighten up their procedures. If hiring someone to be independent, don't let your in-house counsel be involved. Let the player have the opportunity to examine anyone important involved in the investigation. Let them have access to notes. Don't let the independent investigator examine witnesses for you.

What they didn't lose:

  • Goodell appointing himself as the arbitrator.

  • Being able to fully rely on an investigation you initiated as the basis for punishment.
